group.title: Academic life
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: The head of a faculty or college within a university.
examples: The {dean} of medicine welcomed the new students.
wrong: The dean is the newest and most junior student in the college.

words.meaning: Related to the highest university degree.
examples: She is finishing her {doctoral} research in chemistry.
wrong: His doctoral studies were a short course for young children.

words.meaning: A reference to a book, article or author that you have used in your work.
examples: Every quotation needs a full {citation}.
wrong: A citation hides where an idea came from.

words.meaning: To mention a source or author as evidence or support.
examples: Please {cite} at least five academic sources.
wrong: She cited the study by never mentioning it anywhere.

words.meaning: A sentence, usually early in an essay, that states its main argument.
examples: Your {thesis statement} should appear in the first paragraph.
wrong: The thesis statement is a list of sources at the end of the essay.

words.meaning: A short summary at the start of a research paper.
examples: Read the {abstract} first to see if the paper is useful.
wrong: The abstract is the longest chapter of the paper.

words.meaning: A list of all the books and articles used in a piece of writing.
examples: Add the website to your {bibliography}.
wrong: The bibliography lists the author’s favorite foods.

words.meaning: A note at the bottom of a page that gives extra information or a source.
examples: The source is given in a {footnote} on page twelve.
wrong: A footnote is the title printed at the top of the page.

words.meaning: The methods and theory of teaching.
examples: The course covers modern {pedagogy} for language teachers.
wrong: Pedagogy is the study of how plants grow in deserts.

words.meaning: Deep knowledge gained from a great deal of study.
examples: The professor’s {erudition} impressed even her rivals.
wrong: His erudition showed that he had never read a book.

words.meaning: A permanent university teaching post that is hard to lose.
examples: After seven years, the professor was granted {tenure}.
wrong: With tenure, she could be fired at any moment.

words.meaning: An original document or record from the time being studied.
examples: A soldier’s diary is a valuable {primary source} for historians.
wrong: A primary source is a textbook written centuries after the events.

words.meaning: Used as a title for a retired professor who keeps an honorary rank.
examples: He is now professor {emeritus} of physics.
wrong: As an emeritus professor, she had just started her first job.

words.meaning: A place or state where scholars are cut off from real life.
examples: Critics say the researchers live in an {ivory tower}.
wrong: Living in an ivory tower, he knew every problem of ordinary life.

words.meaning: The highest university degree.
examples: She earned her {doctorate} in physics last year.
wrong: A doctorate is the first certificate you get at school.

words.meaning: The main question that a study sets out to answer.
examples: A clear {research question} guides the whole project.
wrong: The research question is the answer printed at the end.

words.meaning: A person who studies a subject in great depth.
examples: She is a leading {scholar} of medieval history.
wrong: The scholar knew almost nothing about any subject.

words.meaning: Showing serious study and learning; written for experts.
examples: The book is a {scholarly} study of ancient trade.
wrong: The scholarly article was a casual blog post with no sources.

words.meaning: A branch of knowledge studied at university.
examples: Linguistics is a fast-growing {discipline}.
wrong: A discipline is a sport played in the university park.

words.meaning: Combining two or more branches of study.
examples: The course takes an {interdisciplinary} approach to climate.
wrong: The interdisciplinary project used only one subject.

words.meaning: A part of a study that sums up and judges earlier research on the topic.
examples: Her {literature review} covers forty earlier studies.
wrong: The literature review discussed only novels she enjoyed on holiday.

words.meaning: To form an idea or model of something in your mind.
examples: The author {conceptualizes} memory as a kind of story.
wrong: He conceptualized the problem without thinking about it at all.

words.meaning: To add notes to a text to explain or comment on it.
examples: Students {annotated} the poem in the margins.
wrong: She annotated the article by leaving it completely untouched.

words.meaning: A period of paid leave given to a university teacher for study or travel.
examples: The professor is on {sabbatical} in Japan this year.
wrong: During her sabbatical, she taught more classes than ever.

words.meaning: To be formally accepted as a student at a university.
examples: She {matriculated} at the university in 2019.
wrong: He matriculated, so he was never accepted onto the course.

words.meaning: A statement that argues against a claim or criticism.
examples: The author published a {rebuttal} to her critics.
wrong: His rebuttal agreed with every point the critics made.

words.meaning: A strong statement that something is true.
examples: The writer gives no evidence for this {assertion}.
wrong: An assertion is a question you ask when you’re unsure.

words.meaning: To read a text carefully to find and correct mistakes.
examples: Always {proofread} your essay before you submit it.
wrong: He proofread the essay by not reading it at all.

words.meaning: Extra material at the end of a book or report.
examples: The full survey questions are in the {appendix}.
wrong: The appendix is the opening sentence of the report.

words.meaning: A detailed book written about one narrow subject.
examples: He published a {monograph} on medieval bridges.
wrong: The monograph covered every subject in the world briefly.

words.meaning: An official record of a student’s courses and grades.
examples: Send a copy of your {transcript} with the application.
wrong: The transcript lists only the student’s favorite songs.

words.meaning: A small class where a teacher discusses work with a few students.
examples: We discussed our essays in the weekly {tutorial}.
wrong: The tutorial was a lecture to a thousand students.

words.meaning: Based on ideas and principles rather than practice.
examples: The course is mainly {theoretical}, with few lab sessions.
wrong: The theoretical course was all hands-on practice.

words.meaning: Honest behavior in study and research, such as not copying or cheating.
examples: Copying answers breaks the rules of {academic integrity}.
wrong: She showed academic integrity by buying an essay online.

words.meaning: To suggest an idea as a basis for an argument or theory.
examples: The paper {postulates} a link between sleep and memory.
wrong: He postulated the idea by refusing to suggest anything.

words.meaning: The ceremony at which students receive their degrees.
examples: Families gathered on the lawn for {commencement}.
wrong: Commencement is the first lecture of the first year.

words.meaning: A paid research post at a university or institute.
examples: She won a two-year research {fellowship} at Oxford.
wrong: The fellowship was a fine she paid for late library books.

words.meaning: A meeting where experts give talks and discuss a subject.
examples: He presented his findings at a {symposium} in Boston.
wrong: The symposium was a quiet place where nobody talked.

words.meaning: A text written by an author before it is printed or published.
examples: She sent the {manuscript} to three journals.
wrong: A manuscript is a book that has already been printed and sold.

words.meaning: Using careful, logical thinking to examine something in detail.
examples: The essay needs a more {analytical} approach.
wrong: His analytical essay simply listed his feelings without reasoning.
